summary: This Standards Track document specifies a Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior for Differentiated Services. It gives a shallow-buffered best-effort service next to the default deep-buffered one, so smooth, low-rate, application-limited flows avoid the delay and loss that queue-building traffic causes. It updates RFC 8325.

plainLanguage.summary: Add a quick lane at a busy store for people with just a few items, so they do not wait behind huge shopping carts.

questions: what dscp is used for nqb
what is a non queue building flow
subtitle: A separate shallow-buffered queue, marked with DSCP 45, so small smooth flows avoid the delay caused by big capacity-seeking ones.

tldr.problem: Low-rate, smooth flows such as voice or game traffic share a deep buffer with capacity-seeking flows that build queues, so they suffer delay, delay variation and loss they did not cause.
tldr.mechanism: Senders mark such flows with DSCP 45, and nodes give them their own shallow queue with the same forwarding preference as Default traffic, plus optional traffic protection against mis-marking.
tldr.outcome: A Proposed Standard that adds the NQB codepoint, gives guidance for DOCSIS, mobile and Wi-Fi, and updates RFC 8325. It promises isolation, not guaranteed delay or rate.

facts.value: 10 ms or less at the shared egress rate

facts.label: Burst bound
facts.value: (R * T) + MTU bytes in any interval T

today: RFC 9956 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It updates RFC 8325, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Shared Queues
sections.content:
RFC 9956 defines the Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior (NQB PHB) for Differentiated Services. It isolates microflows that have relatively low data rates and do not themselves contribute materially to queuing delay and loss. Examples named in the RFC are interactive voice, game sync packets, certain machine-to-machine traffic, DNS lookups and some real-time IoT analytics data.

Common congestion control algorithms such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR seek the available capacity and generally overshoot it, so a queue builds at the bottleneck link. Many bottlenecks also have deep buffers of 100 ms or more. Everyone sharing the link then sees variable delay and loss. Single-queue AQMs help but cannot control the queue much more tightly without hurting throughput, and flow-queuing systems like fq_codel are not suitable for all bottlenecks, for reasons including complexity.

The NQB PHB provides a shallow-buffered, best-effort service as a complement to the Default deep-buffered, best-effort service. A node makes no guarantees on delay or rate beyond the delay bound of the shallow buffer. It is the senders' own behavior that results in low delay and loss.
sections.plainLanguage: When a few people hog the road with big trucks, everyone gets stuck. Giving small bikes their own narrow lane keeps them moving.

sections.title: Queue-Building and Non-Queue-Building Flows
sections.content:
Non-queue-building applications send at low rates or smoothly, so they are unlikely to exceed path capacity even at an inter-packet timescale. Some are transactional and send only a packet or a few per round-trip time. They typically respond to congestion by stopping or sharply reducing transmissions.

Queue-Building (QB) microflows are the opposite. They include flows that probe for link capacity with CUBIC, Reno or other TCP/QUIC congestion control, and flows that send at a high burst rate even if the long-term average is low.

Unlike the Expedited Forwarding PHB, which is the closest relative, NQB has no requirement for a guaranteed minimum rate and no requirement to police to such a rate. NQB is expected to get the same forwarding preference as Default traffic and no better treatment than other classes such as AFxx or EF. The design reduces the incentive to mis-mark because neither higher nor reserved capacity is offered.

The NQB DSCP and PHB operate independently of L4S, but are intended to be compatible with it, so NQB and L4S traffic can share the low-latency queue in an L4S DualQ node.
sections.plainLanguage: Some kids ask for one cookie at a time, and some grab the whole jar. The quick lane is for the one-cookie kids.

sections.title: What Senders Must Do
sections.content:
A microflow is eligible for the NQB DSCP only if it is non-bursty and its rate is limited by the application, at no more than about 1% of the typical network path capacity. It must also be paced: the number of IP bytes sent in any interval T must be at most (R * T) + MTU. At the time of writing, access rates of 50 Mbps or more were typical, which implies an upper limit of 500 kbps.

Applications are RECOMMENDED to use DSCP value 45 (decimal). That value was chosen partly to get separate queuing in existing Wi-Fi networks and partly to make range-based classification in equipment simpler. If a microflow exceeds the rate equation, the application MUST NOT mark it with the NQB DSCP. Microflows are unidirectional, so one application can have both eligible and ineligible flows, such as a video stream and a low-bandwidth control stream in the other direction.

NQB marking does not exempt an application from responding to congestion. It still has to follow guidance such as RFC 8085, and one way to do so is a scalable congestion control mechanism as in RFC 9331. All these requirements concern observable traits of the packet stream, so networks can monitor for misuse and discard or re-mark offending traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: To use the quick lane you must really have only a few items and hand them over one at a time, never in a big armful.

sections.title: What Nodes Must Do
sections.content:
A node supporting the NQB PHB MUST provide a queue for NQB traffic separate from the queue for Default traffic. It SHOULD NOT rate limit or police the NQB aggregate separately from Default traffic. The NQB queue SHOULD get equivalent forwarding preference, for example through a Deficit Round-Robin scheduler with equal weights. The RFC suggests 50% as a reasonable upper bound for the NQB weight in low statistical multiplexing environments.

By default a node SHOULD classify packets with DSCP 45 into the NQB queue, and it MUST support configuring that DSCP. The NQB buffer MUST be significantly smaller than the Default buffer, and the RECOMMENDED size is less than or equal to 10 ms at the shared NQB/Default egress rate. The node MUST also provide statistics, such as packet and drop counters, so operators can detect abuse.

Equipment that serves multiple users SHOULD support per-user provisioning and enforce per-user limits on the aggregate of NQB and QB traffic, so one user's mis-marked traffic does not spread to others.

The incentive design matters: because the NQB queue is small and gives no extra capacity, a QB flow gains little by pretending to be NQB.
sections.plainLanguage: The store gives the quick lane its own small waiting area and the same cashier time as the other lane, so it is fair and nobody gains by cheating.

sections.title: Traffic Protection
sections.content:
A QB flow mis-marked as NQB, by mistake or on purpose, can build a queue that hurts every flow in the NQB queue. So network elements SHOULD support a traffic protection function that spots flows or packets inconsistent with the sender rules and either moves them to the QB queue or discards them. Reclassifying implementations MAY also re-mark such traffic to Default. The RFC does not mandate an algorithm and says decisions SHOULD NOT depend on application-layer data such as ports or addresses, but on the pattern of packet arrivals.

Two styles are described. A per-microflow rate policer uses R equal to 1% of the egress link capacity available for NQB. It is simpler but can be stricter than needed. The alternative detects actual queuing in correlation with each microflow's packets, and RFC 9957 gives an example that keeps per-microflow state for a number of QB microflows (for example 32) and shared state beyond that. The function MUST be designed so the node does not fail if its flow state is exhausted.

If protection is missing, the shallow buffer overflows, and excess packets are redirected to the QB queue or discarded, which degrades correctly marked NQB traffic too. Section 5.3 adds that links which store packets before forwarding, such as PON, Wi-Fi, LTE/5G and DOCSIS, would benefit from limiting the bursts they add, and Section 5.4 requires NQB functions to treat packets uniformly regardless of the ECN field.
sections.plainLanguage: A lane monitor watches for people with giant carts in the quick lane and politely sends them to the regular lane.

sections.title: Deploying NQB Across Networks
sections.content:
Networks and nodes that do not support NQB are RECOMMENDED to treat the NQB DSCP the same as Default, and SHOULD NOT re-mark it, so hops further along can still provide the PHB. Operators may also fold other low-rate, loss-sensitive classes into the NQB queue, such as Telephony and Signaling in RFC 4594 networks, and some equipment may need to aggregate DSCPs 40 to 47.

Across domain boundaries, networks that agree to support NQB SHOULD use DSCP 45 unless the traffic conditioning agreement documents another value. Because DSCP 45 might get high priority in non-DS-capable equipment, operators are RECOMMENDED to re-mark NQB traffic to DSCP 0 before delivery into such a domain, or to apply traffic protection or a policer or shaper. For an aggregate policer or shaper the rate SHOULD be 5% of the interconnection rate or of the typical rate, whichever is greater.

Reordering-sensitive tunnels such as IPsec or L2TP need the outer header re-marked with a non-NQB DSCP, and the pipe model is preferable. For links below 10% of typical path rates, the NQB PHB is RECOMMENDED to be disabled, and the traffic is carried with the Default PHB without re-marking.
sections.plainLanguage: If the next town does not know about the quick lane, you may need to put a plain sticker on your package so it is not wrongly treated as VIP.

sections.title: Mapping NQB to DOCSIS, Mobile and Wi-Fi
sections.content:
For cable broadband, services would need a separate queue for NQB-marked traffic that shares the rate-shaped capacity with the QB queue. For mobile, an LTE network could provide a dedicated low-latency non-GBR EPS bearer, for example QCI 7, and a 5G system could provision a Data Radio Bearer with 5QI 7. Packets with the NQB DSCP would use that path while others use the default bearer.

For Wi-Fi, equipment SHOULD map DSCP 45 into a separate queue in the Best Effort Access Category. It is RECOMMENDED to provide a separate queue in UP 0, and if that is not possible a device MAY use UP 3. Many existing devices use the default DSCP-to-UP mapping, which sends DSCP 45 to UP 5 in the Video Access Category. That gives separate queuing but statistical priority over Best Effort, so the RFC says it is not a compliant PHB implementation and describes ways to limit abuse, such as matching Video EDCA parameters to Best Effort.

RFC 9956 updates RFC 8325. It retitles Section 4.2.9 to "Standard and Non-Queue-Building" and adds a paragraph there, inserts an NQB row in the mapping figure, and adds a sentence to Section 5.3 saying DSCP 45 encodes best-effort service.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of roads, such as cable, phone networks and Wi-Fi, each need their own sign pointing to the quick lane.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security issues concern harm to other flows that share a bottleneck with NQB-marked traffic. Full PHB support with traffic protection limits the incentive for mis-marking, since a mis-marked QB flow would usually see a degradation, such as excessive loss, delay variation or out-of-order delivery, unlike mis-marking for a higher-priority PHB such as EF.

Traffic protection needs flow state, which is finite, so flow-state exhaustion attacks are possible. The RFC requires protection mechanisms to be designed with this in mind, but the outcome depends on the implementation. Per-user provisioning limits keep the effects of shallow buffer overrun from reaching other users.

Diffserv has no integrity protection for the DSCP, so an on-path attacker can change it. The RFC notes that such an attacker could also alter other mutable IP header fields, such as the TTL, which could do much more harm. Existing Wi-Fi networks already give priority to half of the DSCP space, and DSCP 45 would be less attractive for abuse than the other 31 values that get priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Cheating the quick lane does not pay, because it is small and watched, and anyone who tampers with the sticker could do worse things anyway.
